contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Saladin was sultan of Egypt and Syria, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty, and the Muslim ruler most closely associated with the recovery of Jerusalem from the crusader states. Although much of his career unfolded beyond Europe, his actions shaped crusading politics across the medieval Mediterranean.

He defeated the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin, took Jerusalem in 1187, and confronted Richard the Lionheart during the Third Crusade. Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, leaving a reputation for military success, piety, political skill, and a chivalric image that later Christian and Muslim writers both reshaped.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Saladin was born in 1137 or 1138 at Tikrit into a Kurdish family serving military elites in the Islamic world. His family soon moved into the orbit of Zengi and Nur al-Din, rulers whose campaigns against crusader powers shaped Saladin’s early political environment.

He rose through service in Syria and Egypt, initially as part of wider military and administrative networks rather than as an independent ruler. His early career taught him the importance of legitimacy, coalition building, and control of wealthy cities.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Saladin's personality was shaped in memory by both Muslim and Latin writers, which makes him unusually complex. His own biographers, especially Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad and Imad al-Din, emphasised piety, justice, generosity, and Sunni legitimacy, presenting a ruler who wept at the Quran and gave away wealth until his treasury was nearly empty at his death. Later European tradition, remarkably, turned this enemy of the crusaders into a model of chivalric nobility.

That admiration should not erase his political hardness. Saladin was a patient strategist who built power through family appointments, diplomacy, siege warfare, and ideological authority, and who could be ruthless — he executed Reynald of Châtillon with his own hand after the Battle of Hattin and ordered the killing of captured Templars and Hospitallers. His reputation for mercy, above all his restraint after the capture of Jerusalem in 1187, became central to his legend and contrasted deliberately, in the sources, with the massacre that had followed the First Crusade.

The result is a figure who must be read critically: the generous, restrained, devout Saladin is real in the tradition, but he stands beside, not instead of, the calculating dynast who unified Egypt and Syria by force and persuasion. The chivalric myth that later European writers built around him tells us as much about their needs as about the man.

contentSections.title: As sultan of Egypt and Syria
paragraphs: Saladin consolidated power in Egypt, ended the Fatimid caliphate there, and built the Ayyubid dynasty. He then worked to unite Egypt, Syria, and neighboring territories under his authority, presenting his rule as both political restoration and religious duty.

His victory at Hattin in 1187 opened the way to Jerusalem and triggered the Third Crusade. Against Richard the Lionheart, Saladin fought, negotiated, and ultimately accepted a settlement that left Jerusalem under Muslim rule while allowing Christian pilgrimage.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in Damascus in 1193 after illness, leaving the Ayyubid realm to be divided among relatives.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Saladin is remembered as a conqueror of Jerusalem, a unifier of Muslim powers, and a central figure in crusading memory. Medieval and modern traditions often present him as a model of honorable rule, though that image was shaped by literary and political needs.
His legacy matters to European medieval history because crusading culture, diplomacy, and warfare were deeply shaped by his victories and by the challenge he posed to Latin Christian states.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Saladin was born in Tikrit into a Kurdish military family serving in the politics of the Zengid and Abbasid world.

timeline.title: Becomes vizier of Egypt
timeline.description: Rises to power under Nur al-Din's authority.

timeline.title: Ends the Fatimid caliphate
timeline.description: Restores Egypt to Sunni Abbasid allegiance.

timeline.title: Takes Damascus
timeline.description: Begins consolidating Syria and Egypt under Ayyubid rule.

timeline.title: Wins the Battle of Hattin
timeline.description: Crushes the crusader field army and opens the way to Jerusalem.

timeline.title: Captures Jerusalem
timeline.description: Takes the city from the crusader kingdom.

timeline.title: Negotiates with Richard I
timeline.description: Treaty of Jaffa ends the Third Crusade stalemate.

events.title: Siege of Acre
events.label: Besieged the besiegers for two years and lost the port

predecessor.note: Saladin founded the sultanate, abolishing the Fatimid caliphate of Egypt in 1171 and succeeding his nominal overlord Nur ad-Din in Syria

successor.note: Succession shown as Ayyubid sultan. Saladin's lands were first divided among his sons — al-Afdal in Damascus, al-Aziz in Egypt — but his brother al-Adil I outmanoeuvred them and reunited the sultanate, becoming the effective successor.
